output.methodChoice: Applied the framework's sequence internally. Collected X14 (outcomes split by eligibility and work arrangement), then X13 (hiring and exit records) to test the main rival explanation for the tenure gap. No other evidence read.
output.brief:
Short answer: the evidence doesn't support proximity bias as the explanation, and I wouldn't announce the three-office-days rule.

What's going on: policy requires 18 months in your current level before nomination, but the dashboard divides by all staff, including people not yet eligible. Only a third of remote staff (110 of 340) are eligible, versus three-quarters of office staff (560 of 760), because remote hiring opened to all roles only in July 2024 and 215 remote employees joined after February 2025. Among eligible people, nomination (28.6% vs 28.2%), approval (74% vs 71%) and promotion (21.1% vs 20.0%) rates are nearly identical. Job-family mix and attrition (remote 10.9%, office 11.6%) don't explain the gap.

How sure: confident that eligibility timing explains most of it. A small location effect can't be excluded; only 110 remote staff are eligible. Whether remote staff get fewer stretch assignments is untested.

Next: hold the rule, which would also bar about 180 distant home-contract staff without addressing the cause. Report promotion rates for eligible staff, re-check next cycle, and measure how stretch work is allocated before changing it.
